articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo (Kongo) has reached nearly 1,000 suspected cases and over 200 deaths across North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri. The Bundibugyo Ebola virus strain, with no approved vaccine or treatment, has prompted WHO to declare an emergency. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged an immediate ceasefire to curb transmission as mass displacement drives people into crowded refugee camps along the Congo–Uganda border. Attacks on health facilities hinder case finding and contact tracing; shortages of soap, chlorine, and PPE endanger health workers. Donor aid is estimated at about $500 million, yet conflict obstacles limit delivery. Uganda has closed its border with Congo in parts, with entries allowed only in emergencies and a 21-day isolation for entrants; seven Ebola cases have been reported in Uganda, including a death in Kampala. The United States plans to quarantine exposed Americans in Kenya. Tedros plans to visit this week.

articleHeadline: Covid taught us much but Ebola outbreak shows there is work still to be done | The National
articleSummary: As of 28 May 2026, more than 900 suspected Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with more than 100 confirmed deaths and suspected fatalities more than double the confirmed toll. Initial DRC samples were negative, but eight of 13 later tested positive and were identified as the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no vaccine—only supportive care. The outbreak exposes persistent gaps in containment, including weak surveillance, limited laboratory capacity, slow diagnostics and a fragmented international response among governments, NGOs and WHO. West and Central Africa continue to face shortages of trained healthcare workers, PPE and medical supplies. Donor funding has waned, with major funders pulling from WHO and USAID reportedly no longer operating. UK scientists are working to modify a Covid-19 vaccine to target Bundibugyo, underscoring ongoing scientific resourcefulness to stop outbreaks early.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province has caused 220 suspected deaths since it was declared, with only 17 confirmed in the lab. articleHeadline: Tracking Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Spread in China
articleSummary: Drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis spread in China is mapped through decades of whole-genome sequencing and epidemiological modeling, detailing MDR-TB and XDR-TB dynamics across provinces. Analyzed thousands of isolates reveal frontline drug resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin, and fluoroquinolones, with distinct clades emerging independently and multiple introductions fueling regional expansion. Hotspots correlate with population density, healthcare access, and treatment adherence. The study also identifies previously unrecognized mutational pathways conferring resistance to second-line drugs, signaling evolving diagnostic challenges and the need for more precise molecular tests. Spatial analysis shows interprovincial transmission driven by human mobility, urbanization, and socioeconomic factors, challenging static control models and supporting coordinated surveillance. Temporal depth links policy measures to shifts in resistance landscapes, including compensatory mutations that preserve fitness and transmission. Implications favor rapid molecular diagnostics, personalized regimens, and genomics-informed surveillance to curb resistance in China.

articleHeadline: Ebola returns: 5 things most people still don't know about the virus
articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in Congo and Uganda persists. Early Ebola symptoms resemble a generic viral illness (fever, weakness, headaches, muscle aches), which can lead travelers to continue moving before testing. Public behavior—hiding cases, delaying reporting, and risky burial practices—drives transmission, underscoring the importance of trust in health systems and rapid isolation of cases. Israel’s risk is very low; if a case is identified, rapid isolation and contact tracing follow. There is no broad recommendation to avoid flights to Africa; travelers should avoid active outbreak areas, practice hand hygiene, and avoid contact with the sick or contaminated objects. Vaccines and treatments have improved outcomes.

articleSummary: Bepirovirsen, an antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B (HBV), produced a functional cure in 19% of patients across two phase 3 B-Well trials (1,838 participants) treated with weekly injections for 24 weeks, followed by 24 or 48 weeks of nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy; functional cure reached 26% among those with HBV surface antigen <1,000 IU/mL. GSK has submitted for FDA, Japan, Europe, and China approval, with FDA decision expected by October. Mechanistically, bepirovirsen disrupts viral RNA, halts DNA replication, reduces S antigen production, and stimulates innate immunity. Regulatory strategy includes pursuing DAP/TOM (JNJ-3989) and other HBV candidates to broaden cures across viral loads.

No confirmed infections yet; Airport Health Organisation (APHO) teams screen travellers from affected nations, isolate any with even mild symptoms, and send samples to the National Institute of Virology (Pune) for confirmation; results in 24-48 hours. APHO is increasing airport surveillance, tracing travel histories, and using AI-assisted image documentation. In Gujarat, 37-year-old Amuri Lokula, who travelled from Africa and Bangladesh, landed in Mumbai then Vadodara; admitted with fever, cold and cough; moved to an Ebola ward at Ahmedabad Civil Hospital and quarantined. Samples sent to NIV Pune. Lokula’s two business associates and a doctor in contact are under observation. Authorities weighing quarantine, traveller monitoring, and awareness campaigns amid renewed outbreaks in Africa.

The current strain’s behavior remains partly unknown. Transmission is via direct contact with body fluids; the virus persists in corpses, making funeral practices a major driver of spread. Infected individuals shed large viral loads, placing healthcare workers and family caregivers at high risk, especially during late-stage illness when the viral burden peaks. Early symptoms mimic malaria or a cold, but infectiousness peaks after apparent recovery. Death does not render the virus harmless; corpses remain infectious through body fluids and cleansing rituals. Containment is challenged by cross-border movement, ongoing conflict, and distrust of outsiders; safe burial methods using gloves and masks require community acceptance. Past outbreaks were contained by early isolation, but current conditions—mobility and unrest—complicate control.

The outbreak was officially declared on May 15 and has since seen confirmed cases surpass 100 across Ituri, with spillover into North Kivu and South Kivu. On May 27, the first patient exited isolation as the outbreak’s inaugural survivor, amid a context with no approved vaccine or specific therapy for Bundibugyo. Response teams continue aggressive contact tracing, case isolation, and door-to-door sensitization in Mongbwalu, Bunia, and Rwampara, despite security and logistical challenges. Authorities anticipate a potential therapeutic option from an American monoclonal antibody planned for clinical trials. The silent victory of the survivor provides a beacon amid an ongoing, vaccine-free outbreak in eastern DRC, where the outbreak remains active and evolving.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Uganda closes its border with DR Congo due to risk of Ebola outbreak spread.
articleHeadline: Uganda cierra su frontera con RD del Congo por el riesgo de propagación del brote de ébola
articleSummary: Uganda has temporarily closed its border with the Democratic Republic of Congo due to an Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC that has spread into Uganda. The closure is immediate; exceptions apply for authorized Ebola response teams, humanitarian operations, transport of food and goods, and security personnel under strict health controls. Authorized travelers must undergo rigorous health screening, complete location forms, and be monitored at entry. Anyone returning from DRC to Uganda must undertake a 21-day self-isolation under supervision of the Ministry of Health and district surveillance teams. Border districts’ schools remain open but must enforce protocols, identify students who recently returned from DRC, and monitor daily temperatures for 21 days. Districts must designate a health center to host and monitor fever cases awaiting evaluation; media should devote 30 minutes daily to Ebola education. Health authorities report 238 suspected deaths and 1,077 suspected cases in the Congo outbreak; Ituri is the epicenter, with spread to North and South Kivu and into Uganda. Bundibugyo ebolavirus has a 30–50% fatality rate; transmission occurs via direct contact with bodily fluids. The WHO declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on May 17.

articleHeadline: GSK erzielt teilweisen Therapieerfolg mit Hepatitis-B-Wirkstoff
articleSummary: Hepatitis B drug candidate Bepirovirsen by GSK showed partial therapeutic success in two Phase-3 trials. After six months of treatment, 19% of Hepatitis B patients achieved a functional cure, rising to 26% among those with lower viral loads. Results announced May 28, 2026. Current standard therapy often requires lifelong treatment and yields functional cure rates below 1%. GSK CEO Luke Miels aims to accelerate market entry to offset upcoming patent expiries. Regulatory filings have been made in the United States, Japan, China, and Europe; FDA decision is targeted by October 2026. Bepirovirsen is an antisense oligonucleotide designed to halt HBV replication, lower the concentration of a viral antigen in the blood, and boost immune response. The drug was licensed from Ionis Pharmaceuticals.

articleSummary: DR Congo Ebola outbreak in eastern Ituri province, near Uganda and South Sudan, has reached 238 suspected deaths and 1,077 suspected cases as of May 26, 2026, per the Congolese government; WHO reported 222 suspected deaths by May 27. The outbreak, declared May 15, has spread to North and South Kivu and into Uganda, where seven cases have been confirmed in Kampala, including one death; one Congolese case is considered imported, and Uganda has closed its border with the DRC. The circulating strain is Bundibugyo, with a 30–50% case fatality rate; there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. On May 17, the WHO declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern; ten African countries are at high risk due to cross-border spread. Separately in India, four people in Gujarat are quarantined after a Congo traveler developed fever; no confirmed cases yet.

articleSummary: Ebola virus disease (EVD) can begin with subtle symptoms, but in severe cases leads to dangerous complications. Initial signs include weakness, headache and muscle pains, diarrhea and abdominal pain; later stages may feature dry cough and skin rash. As the disease progresses, dehydration and kidney and liver dysfunction can occur, with bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract, nose, gums and other sites in serious cases. The incubation period can reach up to 21 days. If a patient does not improve within 7–16 days of treatment, a critical state may develop, with blood thickening and thrombosis that raise the risk of death. The outbreak situation has prompted strengthened sanitary controls in Central and East Africa. The World Health Organization declared the Ebola situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda an emergency posing a threat to other states.

articleSummary: Mumbai's Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) intensified pre-monsoon mosquito-control targeting dengue and malaria hotspots. On May 28, 2026, the citywide anti-mosquito drive conducted extensive inspections and fogging ahead of rains. The Insecticide Department inspected 32.5 lakh households and fogged around 30.17 lakh households from January through May 27, 2026, while 22,800 area inspections identified breeding grounds. Larvae of Aedes aegypti (dengue) were found at 37,800 locations; Anopheles stephensi (malaria) at 4,529 sites, with all breeding grounds destroyed. Focus areas included overhead tanks, slum-area containers, plastic sheets, flower pots, tyres, coconut shells, and plastic waste. The clean-up removed 540 discarded tyres and over 1.16 lakh scrap items. Campaign extended to about 4,000 redevelopment sites; safety officers trained. Over 1,000 officers and staff, led by Municipal Commissioner Ashwini Bhide, coordinate sustained fogging, spraying, and breeding-site elimination across Mumbai.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Cardiac risk doubles for patients with Chagas disease after surgery.
articleHeadline: Risco cardíaco dobra para pacientes com doença de Chagas após cirurgia
articleSummary: Chagas disease doubles cardiac risk after surgery, based on 378 procedures in 288 patients at the Heart Institute of Hospital das Clínicas, USP, São Paulo (2011–2020). The elevated risk is driven by non-cardiac factors and the complexity of treating Chagas-related cardiomyopathy, not by arrhythmias themselves. Epicardial access was required in ~80% of cases versus 15% for ischemic cardiopathy, increasing intraoperative complications and clinical instability, and thus mortality. Post-discharge care focusing on heart failure and comorbidities is essential, though follow-up varied and some tests (electroanatomic mapping) were not performed in all patients due to budget. Limitations include single-center data and incomplete pharmacologic follow-up over about eight years per patient. Globally, Chagas affects ~7 million people with ~100 million at risk in 21 Latin American countries; 30–40k new cases yearly, with under 10% diagnosed; sporadic cases in North America, Europe, Japan, and Australia.

articleHeadline: Round goby findings in Lake Winnebago prompt emergency rule | Paul A. Smith
articleSummary: An emergency rule in Wisconsin allows unlimited catching and killing of round gobies in Lake Winnebago, after their appearance there in June 2025 near Oshkosh. Approved May 27 by the Natural Resources Board, the rule takes effect after Gov. Evers signs and publishes it, with a hearing in June and a permanent rule planned for fall 2026. Under the rule, gobies may be kept and killed unlimited if eviscerated, decapitated, or with gills removed; anglers are not required to return gobies to water and are urged to report catches to the DNR for monitoring. Gobies are native to Eurasia and established in the Great Lakes, where they can displace native fishes, alter invertebrate communities, and prey on eggs; botulism has been documented in gobies and linked to wildlife mortality. Past barriers slowed spread via Menasha and Neenah dams and the 2015 Menasha Lock closure, but Winnebago remains containment focus.
